messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Omar, a 48-year-old divorced Middle Eastern fashion designer, came to treatment after years of living as if the night of the disaster were still unfolding somewhere just beyond the room he was in. He had been working in his studio, cutting fabric for an upcoming line, when the smell of heat from a steamer and the cool draft from the back door caught his attention in the same instant that a memory of the disaster broke into his mind without warning. He had been inside a building during a man-made disaster years earlier, and what he remembers now arrives in disconnected pieces: a flash of shouting, a jammed doorway, the taste of something bitter and metallic on his tongue, his skin registering a sudden temperature shift that makes his body brace before his mind can organize what is happening. What frightened Omar most was that the memory felt present rather than past, as if he were back in the danger with no clear edge between then and now. When those moments came, nausea would rise sharply, and he would hurt himself physically to release the pressure he felt building inside him, sometimes striking his thigh or gripping his arm hard enough to leave marks. He also threw himself into work with near-constant busyness, staying late at the studio and taking on extra tasks, partly to outrun the image, partly to keep from sitting still long enough for the memory to take hold.

Over time, Omar came to live with the assumption that danger could reappear anywhere and that he would only be safe if he stayed ahead of it. He always identified escape routes before he felt comfortable anywhere, whether he was entering his own studio, a restaurant, or his sister’s apartment, and he constantly scanned his surroundings for signs of danger: exits, crowd density, anything that might slow him down. Even ordinary distractions were difficult because he was so busy tracking doors and windows that he had trouble concentrating on fittings, sketches, or client conversations. Those habits briefly made him feel more prepared, but they also kept him keyed up, and the more he monitored for threat, the more his mind returned to the disaster in those broken, sensory fragments. A taste from the event could come back with startling vividness, and that bodily cue made the scene feel immediate again, which in turn sharpened his sense that he had to keep scanning and planning every move. His repeated checking of locks, doors, and windows was part of the same pattern; he would go back through the apartment several times before bed, then again if he woke during the night, trying to make the world feel containable.

The more Omar tried to manage the distress through these habits, the more tangled the experience became. He noticed that after he hurt himself or buried himself in work, the event seemed to return in even more disjointed flashes, as if the memory had lost whatever fragile order it once had. At the same time, the relief he got from checking and scanning lasted only moments, and the effort left him even more convinced that danger was near. If a memory fragment arrived while he was alone in the studio, he would abandon the fitting room, pace the corridor, and check the back entrance again; if the nausea came on in a client meeting, he would push through with forced busyness and then later search every lock before he could settle. What had begun as an attempt to feel safer had become a daily routine that kept the event active in his mind and body.

Omar’s divorced life had narrowed around these patterns. He avoided inviting people over because he did not want them to notice the repeated checking or the moments when he seemed suddenly far away, and he was embarrassed by how quickly he could lose focus in the middle of a design consultation. He finally sought help after a younger assistant asked him twice in one week whether he was all right, once after Omar stood frozen at the studio door, scanning the hallway and calculating how he would get out if something happened, and again after he absentmindedly injured his arm during a surge of distress. He said he was most afraid that he would never again be able to trust a room, a memory, or even his own body, and he was hoping treatment might help him stop living as though the disaster were still waiting for him at every doorway.
